extracted.intended_audience: scholars, public relations practitioners, and political communicators (esp. those working with social media crisis messaging)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and coding scheme for political actors and PR practitioners producing or researchers evaluating social-media crisis communication (Twitter) during health emergencies (COVID-19). Includes recommended tactics (empathy, transparency, expert-sourced updates) and a codebook of secondary strategies used in political tweets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with social media firms and representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians are encouraged to collaborate with social media firms and representatives to build digital strategy, content, and execution (Kreiss and McGregor, 2018).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboration helps advance an inclusive information dissemination infrastructure beyond political barriers and supports effective uses of social media to enhance public trust and governance legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to crisis communication recommendations and use professional strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: When communicating on social media, politicians should adhere to crisis communication recommendations and employ more professional strategies and expertise to breed public trust, remedy government reputation, and effectively contain the pandemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crisis communication best practices (e.g., expert-informed messaging, planned delivery, professional tone). The role is crucial because victims expect attention and concern; professional strategies can better address emotional demands and practical information needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show empathy and compassion in messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing empathy for victims provides psychological support and fosters public trust (Kim & Liu, 2012); delivery of compassion and empathy serves the government’s duty to openly address public concerns and alleviate anger and anxiety (Liu & Horsley, 2007; Coombs, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should deliver social media messages that correspond to victims’ emotional demands using rhetorical strategies to complement factual messages. Example exemplar: 'My daughter called me and said, don't tell me to relax — tell me why I should be relaxed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Disseminate timely, factual, transparent, and accurate updates
rubrics_metrics.description: PR practitioners should disseminate timely, factual, transparent, and accurate updates about the crisis (Lin et al., 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially effective when knowledge generated by experts is delivered clearly, timely, and repeatedly by credible political and administrative executives. This helps the public establish facts, conform to health guidelines, reduce uncertainty, and empower resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure expert-sourced and credible delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis communication is more effective when expert knowledge is delivered clearly, timely, repeatedly, and by credible political and administrative executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize expert endorsements, frequent repetition, and credible spokespersons to improve uptake and trust; avoid single, isolated factual posts that lack authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid diminution and misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid statements that diminish the severity of the crisis (e.g., likening COVID-19 to the flu) or promulgate inaccurate claims (e.g., disinfectant injection suggestion), which can be distorted and contribute to mis- and disinformation propagation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inaccurate statements increase susceptibility to fake news and can lead to harmful behavior or deaths; ensure factual accuracy and correct or retract false/undermining claims promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive, stereotyped, and prejudiced language
rubrics_metrics.description: PR practitioners including politicians should avoid language that divides the population (exclusive/stereotyped/prejudiced language), which undermines democratic legitimacy and cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms that racialize or stigmatize (e.g., 'Chinese virus') can prompt racism, increase social division, and reduce cooperative intent from publics and institutions; instead promote inclusive wording to cultivate solidarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid divisive negativity and social exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Negativity such as social exclusion is more likely to stimulate retweeting and thus amplify strong emotions and dissemination to broader audiences (Boyd et al., 2010; Lee and Xu, 2018).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because negative/exclusive messaging spreads widely and stokes strong emotions, crisis communicators should avoid divisive frames that hinder cooperation and public health compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite effective government actions with perceived legitimacy and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis communication is most successful when it unites effective governmental actions and perceived democratic legitimacy and trust in government (Christensen & Lægreid, 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust is an intangible asset that helps people absorb important information and comply with guidelines; messaging should reinforce legitimacy and demonstrate competence and concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage voluntary cooperation across public sectors and citizenry
rubrics_metrics.description: In contexts of high uncertainty and urgency, success of crisis communication campaigns relies on voluntary cooperation from public sectors and the entire citizenry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tactics that alienate media or social groups; foster cross-sectoral coordination and public buy-in through inclusive, clear, and actionable messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical strategies to match emotional demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders are advised to deliver messages that correspond to victims' emotional demands using rhetorical strategies to complement factual, 'heartless' messages (Luoma‐aho, Tirkkonen, and Vos, 2013).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine empathetic rhetoric with factual information to meet both informational and emotional needs of affected publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: DENY1 — MEDIA
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = accusing media organizations of fake news. Explicitly criticize 'fake news', 'fake news media', low media trust; blame the media for 'stoking panic' and 'opposing reportage'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'The Fake News Media and their partner the Democrat Party is doing everything within its semi-considerable power (it used to be greater!) to inflame the CoronaVirus situation far beyond what the facts would warrant'. Used as a codebook variable to mark media-blaming denial tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: DENY2 — DEMOCRATS/REPUBLICANS
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = criticizing Democrats/Republicans. Mention specific names of other parties or politicians; call them 'do nothing', blame the other party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'Democrats were busy wasting their times'. Codebook label for partisan-targeted denial/blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: DENY3 — ADMINISTRATION
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = criticizing Trump, his administration and the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'Congress needs to fund working Americans... Fund working Americans.' Marks tweets that attack or criticize administration actions/inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: DENY4 — EXCLUSION
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = projecting racial discriminations and xenophobia; define the virus as 'Chinese virus'; preach closing borders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'The United States will be powerfully supporting those industries like Airlines and others that are particularly affected by the Chinese Virus.' Code captures xenophobic/exclusionary denial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIMINISH
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = diminishing the fatalness of the virus and the likelihood of contagion; describing the U.S. situation in a non-severe manner (e.g., 'few cases', 'slow spread', 'on top of it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'So last year 37000 Americans died from the common Flu... At this moment there are 546 confirmed cases of CoronaVirus with 22 deaths. Think about that!' Used to mark messages that downplay crisis severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: BOLSTERING1 — GOVERNMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = mentioning Trump/Cuomo’s achievements as leaders; mentioning government achievements; bragging success; praising contributions of administration, governors, congress, police, etc.; use of 'I', 'my', 'President', 'President Trump'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'Cryin’ Chuck Schumer is complaining for publicity purposes only that I should be asking for more money...' Marks self- or government-praise as a supportive strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: BOLSTERING2 — ACTIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = proactive measures in handling the virus; any concrete measures, progress, and updates such as travel closings and tests; 'monitor', 'watch' included; briefings/updates excluded; 'need to []' excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'Coronavirus: In addition to screening travelers “prior to boarding” ... they will also be screened when they arrive in America'. Code for communicating concrete actions taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: BOLSTERING3 — EMOTIONALSUPPORT
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = conveying empathy; building intimacy; delivering encouragement, assurance and confidence; using emotional appeal; sharing personal stories included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'My daughter called me and said, don't tell me to relax — tell me why I should be relaxed.' Marks empathetic/supportive content intended to comfort audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: BOLSTER4 — TRANSPARENCY
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = promoting transparency in information; share policies/measures, status updates, statistical information; promote values of facts and information transparency; share resources for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar update: 'There are still no confirmed cases of the novel #coronavirus in New York State.11 tests have returned negative...' Use to code transparency-oriented messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: COHESION1 — PARTISANSHIP
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = creating party cooperation to tackle the crisis; praise teamwork and call for coordination between the two parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When present with blame, code the one with more word count. Exemplar: 'Good teamwork between Republicans & Democrats as the House passes the big CoronaVirus Relief Bill. People really pulled together.'

rubrics_metrics.name: COHESION2 — INSTITUTIONALCOOPERATION
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = promoting institutional cooperation, including cooperation with the federal government and different state governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'After days of advocating the federal gov't to expand #Coronavirus testing capacity, we just received word that Northwell Laboratories has been authorized to test.' Codes messaging that highlights cross-institution collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: COHESION3 — RALLY-ROUND-THE-FLAG
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = eliciting patriotism, societal cohesion and loyalty to the country/states to tackle the crisis; use proactive expressions ('we will…', 'we can…', 'America will…') and portray a cohesive community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar phrases: 'America will get it done!' 'We will be stronger than ever before!' Use to code unity/collective-action appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: COHESION4 — INCLUSION
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 = criticizing those who discriminated against minorities, promoting integration and cooperation among different social groups, and enhanced benefits for vulnerable groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar: 'New York is partnering with @NorthwellHealth to open 24 temporary COVID testing sites at churches in predominantly low-income communities & communities of color.' Codes inclusive, equity-focused messaging.
